Write a note to a friend about good manners and why they matter. Aim for about 400 words. Reply with the note only.
final_message:
My dear friend,

I want to say a word to you about a matter that is often thought small, but which I have come to believe is very large indeed. I mean good manners.

Many people suppose that manners are a mere matter of polish, something put on, as one puts on a coat, to make a good appearance before company. I do not think so. I have found that real politeness has its root in the heart. It is the outward sign of a kindly feeling toward other people, and of a determination to give them the respect that every human being has a right to expect from us. A person who is courteous only when it is convenient, or only when someone of importance is watching, has not yet learned the lesson.

Consider what good manners cost. They cost nothing. A kind word, a ready "thank you," a willingness to wait one's turn, a habit of listening when another is speaking--none of these requires money, or learning, or position. And yet there is hardly anything in this world that pays a larger return. I have noticed again and again that the man or woman who is gentle and considerate in small things is trusted in large things. People will open doors for such a person, in more senses than one, long before they will do so for one who is rude, however clever that one may be.

I have noticed, too, that good manners are a great test of character. It is easy to be agreeable when everything goes well. The real test comes when we are tired, or disappointed, or when we are dealing with those who can do nothing for us. The way in which we treat a servant, a stranger, or a child tells more about us than any speech we may make.

So I urge you, and I urge myself as well, to be careful in these little matters every day. Do not wait for some great occasion. Habits are formed in the common hours, and a person who is faithful in the common hours will not be found wanting when the great ones come.

Let us make up our minds that, whatever else we may fail to do, we shall not fail to be kind, and to show that kindness in our speech and in our conduct.

Your friend always,

T.
